correctness.rationale: For \(\alpha>-1\), the normalized beta-integral moments yield \(h_m=\Gamma(m+\beta+1)/(\Gamma(\beta+1)\Gamma(m+1))\), strictly increasing and regularly varying with exponent \(\beta=\alpha+1\). Every orbit vector is an explicit scalar multiple of a single normalized monomial, so Tonelli gives exactly \(\Lambda_m=\sum_{s_j\le m}h_{s_j}/h_m\) and the optimal frame bounds. The jump equation forces \(B_\infty-A_\infty\ge1\), and the ratio \(\Lambda_{s_j}/\Lambda_{s_{j+1}-1}=h_{s_{j+1}-1}/h_{s_j}\), combined with gamma-ratio asymptotics, proves \(\limsup s_{j+1}/s_j\le\kappa_\infty^{1/\beta}\). Iteration yields the sharp logarithmic density. Geometric spacing attains both limiting extremal diagonals for every \(\kappa>1\); the dyadic unweighted example gives optimal global constants. The embedded checker passes twelve independent finite comparisons and 4,095 dyadic entries, supplementary only.

value.rationale: The natural cost of a countable dynamical sampling system is how many unit-norm monomial sensors are placed below a specified degree; its useful stability invariant is the high-degree frame-bound ratio. Across every weighted Bergman space with \(\alpha>-1\), the claim resolves the sharp analytic density-versus-condition tradeoff over all increasing sets of normalized monomial generators, with geometric placement optimal for every prescribed \(\kappa>1\). This is a structural classification of attainable sparsity/conditioning, beyond mere frame existence or isolated computation; the nonmonomial class is excluded explicitly.
